name: Tegid

attributes.attribute: the Welsh name for what is now Lake Bala
brewed her magical potion there in a cauldron
swallowed some brew and won wisdom and poetic talent
reborn from the goddess after she ate Gwion

sources: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
text: Tegid is a Welsh mythological site. The place now called Lake Bala in north Wales appears in myth as Llyn Tegid. It was the home of the great goddess Ceridwen. She brewed her magical potion there in a cauldron. She left a boy named Gwion to watch it. Gwion swallowed some of the brew by accident. He gained wisdom and poetic talent. He then fled. The all knowing Ceridwen knew what happened and chased him. She ate him at last. She then gave birth to him as the great bard Taliesin. People thought Lake Bala was so deep that no one could measure it. Anyone who tried heard a booming voice. The voice said the measurement must stop. Dragons were said to live in the deep lower parts.

okr.objective: Describe Tegid, the Welsh sacred lake site.
key_results: Tegid appears as Llyn Tegid, the home of the goddess Ceridwen.
Gwion tasted her brew, gained wisdom, and fled, then was eaten and reborn as Taliesin.
Legend said Lake Bala's depth could not be measured and that dragons dwelled below.
okr.evidence: Monaghan, Patricia. The Encyclopedia of Celtic Mythology and Folklore. Checkmark Books, 2008.
